item.title: Sources & interpretations
item.description:
On this paper the interpretation question tests AO4 — how interpretations differ, why they differ, and which is more convincing. The key to why they differ is provenance: who wrote it, when, their background and purpose.

Below is the provenance of every interpretation AQA has set. Read it and ask: how might this author’s background, date and purpose explain the view they take?

2024

Interpretation A (Questions 1–3)

The American Civil War was fought over the issue of slavery. The North believed in human rights and freedom. In the South there was an illegal government based only on the rights of the strongest. The Civil War was started by clever speech makers and traitors in the South who decided to break up the United States. The South was to blame for its own suffering in the War and the North won because it had right on its side.

Provenance: Adapted from a speech by Frederick Douglass in 1878. Douglass was a slave until 1838 when, aged 20, he escaped. He became a leading figure in the campaign to abolish slavery. In 1881 he published his best-selling autobiography. Douglass was speaking on 30 May – 'Decoration Day' – when soldiers from the North who died in the Civil War were remembered.

item.title: How to answer the 12-mark question ("Which was more important?")
item.description:
What this question is

  • It is always Question 6 on the American West paper, and at 12 marks it is the biggest single question on this section. (The American West paper has no 16-mark question — that only appears on the depth studies.)
  • It gives you a statement with two bullet points and asks which was the more important reason, cause or consequence.
  • It tests your knowledge (AO1) and your ability to analyse and reach a judgement (AO2). It is marked on history only — there are no separate marks for spelling and grammar.

What the examiner is looking for

Level Marks What it looks like
4 10–12 Explains both bullets with accurate detail, brings in knowledge beyond the bullets, and sustains an argument that reaches a justified overall judgement.
3 7–9 Explains both bullets with good knowledge — but the judgement is weak, bolted on, or missing.
2 4–6 Simple explanation; mostly describes rather than explains importance.
1 1–3 Basic, general points; little accurate detail.

The single thing that separates Level 4 from Level 3: a judgement that runs through the whole answer, not a “both were important” sentence tacked on at the end.

item.title: Overview
item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Homestead Act (1862)
    • At the time — opened the Plains to mass settlement
    • Long term — drove conflict with Native Americans
  • Transcontinental Railroad (1869)
    • At the time — connected East to West
    • Long term — accelerated buffalo slaughter and Native displacement
  • Indian Wars (1860s–90s)
    • At the time — series of military conflicts
    • Long term — ended Native American independence on the Plains

Key knowledge — DSTEP

Type Item Why it matters
Date 1830 Indian Removal Act — US government begins forcible displacement of Native Americans
Date 1840s Oregon Trail migration — mass westward movement begins
Date 1862 Homestead Act — free land offered to settlers willing to farm the Plains
Date 1869 Transcontinental Railroad completed — transformed the Plains forever
Date 1890 Wounded Knee Massacre — symbolic end of the Indian Wars
Stat 2,000 miles Length of the Oregon Trail — the primary route west
Stat ~600,000 Native American population around 1800 — halved by 1900
Stat 160 acres Land granted to homesteaders under the Homestead Act 1862
Term Manifest Destiny Belief that American expansion westward was God-given and inevitable
Term Homesteader Settler farming the Great Plains under the Homestead Act
Term Plains Indians Native peoples of the Great Plains — nomadic, buffalo-dependent
Term Reservation Defined land parcels where Native Americans were confined
Person President Andrew Jackson Signed Indian Removal Act 1830 — set the pattern of forced displacement
Person Sitting Bull Hunkpapa Lakota leader — symbol of Native resistance
Person General Custer Led 7th Cavalry — defeated at Little Bighorn 1876; became a symbol of the Indian Wars

item.title: Migration across the Great Plains (12-mark)
item.description:
12-mark question · Which was more important · AO1/AO2

The question

Which of the following was the more important reason why white Americans travelled across the Great Plains in the 1840s and 1850s:

  • religion
  • economic opportunity?

Explain your answer with reference to both reasons. [12 marks]

Compare the levels below — same question, different grades. Notice what the higher-level answer does that the lower one doesn’t.

Model answer — Level 3

Religion was a very important reason as to why the white Americans travelled across
the Great Plains in the 1840s and 50s. For example, the Mormons travelled west to get away from those who were against the Mormon religion. Polygamy was one of
the practises of the Mormon religion that many other Americans didn’t understand and didn’t like. Also the fact that the holy book was considered blasphemy lead to many Mormons being harmed or worse if they stayed in the East. So, they left and went across the Great Plains to the Great Salt Lake to avoid discrimination against
them.
Yet, economic opportunity called more groups of people across the Great Plains as the East held so much potential. The miners went through the Great Plains during the
Californian gold rush because many young men though that they could get their
fortune form the gold that appeared to be in abundance in the West. Also, the pioneers travelled across the Great Plains in search of more room for them to have and more land for them to own for a cheaper price. Many mining towns opened up across the West, which enticed many young men as they had little to no law enforcement and a lot of gambling and brothels for the to explore. This was an important reason because it lead to so many people moving across the Great Plains
to find their fortune.

item.title: Plains Indians: impact of white settlers (8-mark)
item.description:
8-mark question · In what ways · AO1/AO2

The question

In what ways were the lives of Indians affected by the arrival of white settlers on the Great Plains? [8 marks]

Compare the levels below — same question, different grades. Notice what the higher-level answer does that the lower one doesn’t.

Model answer — Level 3

The lives of the Indians were affected by the arrival of the white settlers on the Great
Plains because they were forced to adapt slightly to the white lifestyle by having to live side by side along with them when they never had before. If they didn’t, there
was often conflict between the two groups due to misunderstandings of each other.
As more white s ettlers moved further west, the Indians were forced out of their Indian Territory which they had been used to living in and moved even further west. If they
didn’t move freely they were removed by force, such as in the ‘Trail of Tears’, where thousands of Indians died along the way. Also, their land was broken up into lots of smaller areas, spread out across the country. This made it difficult for the Indians to hunt buffalo because if they were
hunting them and they went out of their boundary the Indians would have to give up. The smaller pieces of land had a big effect on the Indians nomadic lifestyle as they couldn’t move around as much or as freely as they wanted to.

item.title: Geography of the Plains
item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • First crossings (1840s) — Oregon Trail migrants cross the Plains — at the time: obstacle; later: territory to settle
  • Transcontinental Railroad (1869)
    • At the time — crossed the Plains
    • Long term — made the Plains accessible and attractive to settlers

Key knowledge — DSTEP

Type Item Why it matters
Date 1840s First wagon trains cross the Plains — seen as a wasteland to pass through, not settle
Date 1869 Transcontinental Railroad — crosses the Plains and changes perception entirely
Stat 500,000 sq miles Size of the Great Plains — vast, treeless, seemingly inhospitable
Stat Under 20 inches Annual rainfall — why early settlers called it the “Great American Desert”
Stat -40°C to 43°C Extreme temperature range — one of the core challenges for homesteaders
Term Great Plains Vast grassland stretching from Mississippi to the Rockies — the central geography of this unit
Term Treeless Prairie No timber for building or fuel — a major problem for early settlers
Term Grassland Supported vast buffalo herds and Plains Indian nomadic life
Term Sod Compressed earth used for building “sodbusters’” homes — adaptation to lack of timber
Person Plains Indians Adapted perfectly to the Plains — nomadic life followed the buffalo
Person Early migrants Treated the Plains as a barrier — the change to viewing it as desirable land is key

Think like a historian

What does calling the Plains a “desert” reveal about the perspective of the people using that word?

item.title: Mormons: settlement at Great Salt Lake (4-mark)
item.description:
4-mark question · Describe two problems · AO1

The question

Describe two problems faced by the Mormons when they settled at the Great Salt Lake. [4 marks]

Compare the levels below — same question, different grades. Notice what the higher-level answer does that the lower one doesn’t.

Model answer — Level 2

The Mormons faced many problems when they settled at the Great Salt Lake. The Great Salt Lake was in the middle of a desert, so they had to find water and establish
a supply system to feed the people and water the crops. The second problem was how to divide the land between the settlers. The bigger farms went to people with families, so this could cause tension between the settlers.

item.title: Sand Creek Massacre (4-mark)
item.description:
4-mark question · Interpretations: differences · AO4a/AO4b

The question

How does Interpretation B differ from Interpretation A about the attack on the Indian camp at Sand Creek?
Explain your answer using Interpretations A and B.
[4 marks]

The interpretations / sources

Interpretation A (George Bent) — provenance

  • George Bent in a letter to the historian George Hyde, sent between 1905 and 1918.
  • Bent was born in 1843. He had a Cheyenne Indian mother and a white father who ran the local trading post at Sand Creek. In 1864 he was staying with his mother’s relatives at Sand Creek.

Interpretation A text The Indians at Sand Creek were friendly and under the protection of Fort Lyon. However, Chivington had been planning this attack for weeks… Chivington’s troops were the worst sort of frontier whites… united only by their eagerness to kill Indians.

item.title: Push or Pull Me West
item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Oregon Trail migration (1840s)
    • At the time — religious/economic migration
    • Long term — opened the West to permanent settlement
  • Gold Rush (1848)
    • At the time — massive pull factor
    • Long term — California’s population explosion; westward momentum
  • Homestead Act (1862)
    • At the time — free land
    • Long term — accelerated displacement of Plains Indians

Key knowledge — DSTEP

Type Item Why it matters
Date 1840s Oregon Trail at peak use — religious and economic push/pull factors driving migration
Date 1848 Gold Rush — pull factor of enormous power draws 80,000 in one year
Date 1862 Homestead Act — government-created pull factor; free land
Stat 300,000 Used Oregon Trail by 1870 — scale of voluntary migration west
Stat 2,000 miles Length of Oregon Trail — the journey itself was a push/pull test
Stat $10 Filing fee under Homestead Act — low barrier to land ownership
Term Push factors Reasons people left: poverty, unemployment, religious persecution, land exhaustion
Term Pull factors Reasons people moved west: free land, gold, religious freedom, adventure
Term Manifest Destiny Ideological pull — religious and national duty to settle the continent
Term Oregon Trail 2,000-mile route west — the physical embodiment of push/pull migration
Person Pioneer families Driven by combination of push and pull — students must be able to distinguish both
Person President Lincoln Signed Homestead Act — turned land into the ultimate pull factor

item.title: The Mormons and Joseph Smith
item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Church founded (1830)
    • At the time — small new religious movement
    • Long term — became one of America’s most significant religious communities
  • Smith killed (1844)
    • At the time — sparked migration crisis
    • Long term — Brigham Young leads Mormons to Utah, creating a permanent community

    • At the time — religious exodus
    • Long term — established a thriving community in an “empty” territory

Key knowledge — DSTEP

Type Item Why it matters

Date 1844 Joseph Smith killed by a mob in Carthage, Illinois
Date 1847 Brigham Young leads Mormons to Great Salt Lake, Utah
